conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen during pregnancy and after a baby arrives.  

To get a quick, gentle snapshot of how you’ve been feeling lately, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the EPDS—short for Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days, and it helps us see if you might benefit from a little extra support right now.  

Everything you share stays between you and the care team unless you tell us something that suggests immediate safety concerns; then we pull in extra help to keep you safe. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll go at your pace. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first of the ten questions, and we’ll just have a conversation.  

Shall we begin?  

Over the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt for you?

[soft half-shrug, eyes on the floor]

I still laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent that silly video—but it feels… distant, I guess. It’s almost like I have to remind myself to chuckle, and the laughter fades really fast. Things that used to crack me up for hours now give me maybe a second or two before the heaviness comes back.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[eyes flick up, then back down]

Most of the time, no… not really. I’ll smile if someone else is laughing, but it doesn’t feel natural—more like I’m acting.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to get excited when my mom offers to take me for coffee or when my favorite show drops a new episode, but… it’s flat. I go through the motions, hoping the spark will come back, but mostly I just feel numb or worried about the baby.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If he spits up more than usual, or if he won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I know rationally it’s not all on me, but the guilt just barges in anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[slow exhale, rocking the stroller slightly with my foot]

Pretty much all the time. I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly my heart’s racing—is he breathing? Is that rash getting worse? Did I sterilize the bottle right? Nothing major even has to happen for the worry to hit. It’s like my mind’s always scanning for danger, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—usually at night—this wave of fear just slams into me. My chest feels tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. Dishes pile up, the laundry never ends, and every time I check one thing off, three more appear. I keep telling myself, “Just get through the next hour,” but it’s exhausting.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet voice, rubbing my thumb along the stroller handle]

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying I missed something with the baby. It takes me forever to drift off, and when I finally do, I wake up with my heart pounding for no reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes. It’s there most of the day—this heavy, gray feeling. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start sliding down without me even noticing right away. It’s like the sadness sits on my chest and won’t move.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once this morning—everything felt like too much and I just sat on the nursery floor crying while he napped. Another night I couldn’t stop after my partner asked if I was okay.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice drops]

Once or twice, just a quick flash—like “what if I weren’t here.” I’ve never planned anything, never wanted to leave my baby, but the thought flickers in when everything feels hopeless. It scares me, so I push it away fast.

You've shared how the joy that used to come easily now feels out of reach: laughter feels forced, outings seem flat, and a heavy, gray sadness sits on your chest most of the day. You're working so hard to be a good mother-yet waves of worry, guilt, and sudden panic keep crashing over you, especially at night when you long for sleep. Feeling overwhelmed and occasionally haunted by fleeting thoughts of escape, you still bravely show up for your baby, and reaching out today shows real strength.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh naturally and only feigning amusement when others laugh, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states she feels 'flat,' 'numb,' and only 'goes through the motions' without experiencing genuine enjoyment, aligning with 'Hardly at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive self-blame ('a lot of the time') that intrudes despite rational awareness, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, unprovoked worry and intrusive thoughts, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense nocturnal panic attacks that leave her breathless and convinced something awful is imminent, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty managing daily tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing thoughts and anxiety, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two distinct crying episodes explicitly linked to feeling "unhappy" and "everything felt like too much," matching "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the cutoff where <med>postpartum depression</med> is probable. Core symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: daily depressed mood and diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) nearly all day, tearfulness, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, recurrent anxiety and panic attacks, sleep disruption unrelated to infant needs, and passive suicidal ideation (Q10 ≥1). The combination meets clinical threshold for urgent mental-health assessment and safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental-health crisis clinic</med> for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional support is in place; avoid being alone if thoughts of harm reappear
3. Call 988 (US Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if self-harm urges intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Begin gentle daily structure: one small goal (shower, 10 min outside, balanced snack) to support recovery while awaiting care
5. Consider sharing today's results with your partner or family so they can help coordinate appointments and nighttime support
6. Limit internet symptom-searching; instead, use trusted resources like Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773) for guidance and local providers
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-anchored interview):
- Marked anhedonia: absent/forced laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days, multiple crying episodes this week
- Excessive guilt re infant care (“I must be doing something wrong”)
- Chronic, intrusive anxiety (cardiac awareness, safety scanning) and nocturnal panic attacks
- Sleep-onset difficulty driven by rumination; middle insomnia with spontaneous panic
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “barely treading water” with daily tasks
- Passive self-harm cognitions (“what if I weren’t here”) without plan or intent

Pattern: symptoms present >2 weeks, interfere with functioning and attachment experiences; highest intensity evenings/nights.

Risk indicators: positive for items 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 → total score range 16–19 (estimated high screening range). Passive suicidal ideation endorsed; requires immediate safety assessment per protocol.

Screening significance: findings consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; rule-out perinatal mood & anxiety disorder, evaluate for safety plan and expedited referral.
